Abstract: In China, close to half of the population is overweight (body mass index [BMI] 25-29.9 kg/m2) or obese (BMI ≥30 kg/m2).1, 2 Obesity is associated with higher risks of developing type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), hypertension, dyslipidaemia, cardiovascular disease and orthopaedic problems, and reduces life expectancy. Although lifestyle modification (diet and exercise) represents the first line of weight management, weight loss over the long term has been difficult to maintain. Despite the importance of weight management in improving health outcomes for obese or overweight patients, relatively few pharmacotherapies are approved for weight management, and many have been associated with serious adverse events (SAEs).3, 4 Semaglutide is a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) analogue that is approved at doses up to 1 mg, administered subcutaneously once weekly for the treatment of T2DM, and is recommended as a second-line therapy after metformin. Furthermore, meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of semaglutide in patients with T2DM have shown benefits of the drug on glycaemic control and weight loss.5, 6 Recently, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the use of semaglutide for patients with obesity or overweight, and many studies7-9 that tested the efficacy and safety of semaglutide in the treatment of obesity or overweight have been published. Nevertheless, there is still a lack of comprehensive evaluation of the available evidence to support the use of semaglutide for obese or overweight patients in clinical practice. This study was designed to provide an overview of the beneficial and harmful effects of semaglutide in obese or overweight patients. Our meta-analysis protocol is registered on PROSPERO (CRD42021259374). Neither ethics approval nor patient consent was required for this analysis. The literature was comprehensively searched through PubMed, Embase and Cochrane Library from the inception of each database to 18 May 2021. The search used text and medical subject headings including semaglutide, Wegovy, obesity, and overweight. ClinicalTrials.gov and the references of selected studies and reviews were also reviewed manually. The strategies are available in Supplementary Table S1. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (a) RCT design; (b) inclusion of a population of adults with obesity or overweight; (c) intervention with semaglutide; (d) comparison with a placebo; (e) reporting of any of the efficacy outcomes, such as evaluation of quality of life (36-item short-form health survey [SF-36] physical functioning score or impact of weight on quality of life-Lite clinical trials (IWQOL-Lite-CT) physical function score) or decreased body weight and safety endpoints; (f) inclusion of weight-related coexisting conditions such as hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea or cardiovascular disease was permitted; and (g) minimum treatment duration of 12 weeks. Conference abstracts, letters, case reports and comment papers were excluded. If the same trial was published in different journals it was included only once. The studies which involved obesity or overweight patients with or without diabetes were included in this meta-analysis. Two investigators independently assessed trial eligibility by screening titles/abstracts and full texts. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus with a senior researcher. Two investigators independently extracted data using a standardized form, and disagreements were resolved by consensus after discussion. Extracted data included baseline characteristics, the outcomes of interest and quality assessment of the included studies. The quality of each study was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Assessment for RCTs.10 Percentage change in body weight and weight reduction of at least 5% were primary outcomes in this meta-analysis. The primary and secondary outcomes were both evaluated at the end of treatment, and the detailed time points for each study are listed in Table S2. All analyses were performed using RevMan5.4 software and Stata16.0 software. Mean difference (MD) or risk ratio (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were used to assess the outcomes. Pooled analyses were performed using a random-effects model. We applied the LFK index to estimate possible publication bias. We performed subgroup analysis according to different doses of semaglutide and meta regression to verify the dependency of the percentage change in body weight and weight reduction of at least 5% on age, female ratio, BMI, glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c), and diabetes rates in different studies. The robustness of the meta-analysis models was further tested in sensitivity analyses using leave-one-out methods. We identified 455 potentially eligible references using the initial searches. After removal of duplications, we retrieved 404 relevant references. Subsequent abstract screening of the remaining 404 references resulted in the exclusion of all but nine studies. Finally, we found seven studies7-9, 11-14 that were eligible for inclusion. The process of study selection is shown in Figure 1. The basic characteristics of the included studies and patients are presented in Table S2. Random sequence generation and allocation concealment were adequate in six trials8, 9, 11-14 and were evaluated as being at low risk of selection bias. Seven trials were double-blind, and none of the trials were terminated prematurely. There was no evidence of reporting bias according to published trial protocols. All trials were free of performance bias, detection bias, attrition bias and reporting bias. Other sources of bias were unclear in all the included studies. Details regarding the risk-of-bias assessment are summarized in Figure S1. Data on the percentage change in body weight were available for 4824 participants from five studies. Semaglutide significantly decreased body weight compared with placebo (MD −10.55%, 95% CI −14.13% to −6.96%; P < 0.00001 [Figure S2]). There was minor asymmetry according to the LFK index (1.04, minor asymmetry). Five studies (n = 4724) reported data for weight reduction of at least 5%. The pooled analysis showed that, compared with those in the placebo group, more participants in the semaglutide group achieved a weight reduction of at least 5% (RR 2.29, 95% CI 1.88-2.80; P < 0.00001 [Figure S3]). No evidence of publication bias was identified via the LFK index (−0.02, no asymmetry). Semaglutide significantly reduced body weight (kg) compared with placebo (MD −9.39 kg, 95% CI −12.21 kg to −6.57 kg; P < 0.00001) (Figure S4). There was no asymmetry according to the LFK index (0.26, no asymmetry). The analysis results indicated that semaglutide resulted in more patients achieving a reduction in body weight of 10% or more compared to placebo (RR 4.30, 95% CI 3.20-5.78; P < 0.00001 [Figure S5]). There was major asymmetry based on the LFK index (−2.61, major asymmetry). The pooled analysis suggested that semaglutide was superior to placebo in terms of a reduction in body weight of 15% or more (RR 6.67, 95% CI 4.67-9.55; P < 0.00001 [Figure S6]). Based on the LFK index (−3.18, major asymmetry), there was evidence of publication bias among the included studies. Patients in the semaglutide group had a smaller waist circumference (cm) than those in the placebo group (MD −7.35 cm, 95% CI −9.85 cm to −4.84 cm; P < 0.00001 [Figure S7]). Assessment of data using the LFK index (2.63, major asymmetry) indicated major publication bias. Patients treated with semaglutide had a significantly lower systolic blood pressure than those in the control group (MD −4.20 mmHg, 95% CI −5.07 mmHg to −3.33 mmHg; P < 0.00001 [Figure S8]). Minor publication bias was found (LFK index = 1.28, minor asymmetry). The pooled analysis showed that, compared with the placebo group, the semaglutide group had a much higher SF-36 physical functioning score (MD 1.66, 95% CI 1.07-2.26; P < 0.00001 [Figure S9]). There was evidence of minor publication bias among the included studies based on the LFK index (−1.24, minor asymmetry). The analysis results indicated that semaglutide was superior in the change in IWQOL-Lite-CT physical function score (MD 6.12, 95% CI 2.10-10.13; P = 0.003 [Figure S10]). There was evidence of publication bias among the included studies based on the LFK index (−3.83, major asymmetry). As shown in Figure S11, semaglutide increased the incidence of AEs compared to placebo (RR 1.06, 95% CI 1.01-1.12; P = 0.03). Publication bias was absent (LFK index = −0.32, no asymmetry). As shown in Figure S12, semaglutide increased the incidence of SAEs compared to placebo (RR 1.34, 95% CI 1.02-1.77; P = 0.04). Based on the LFK index (−0.02, no asymmetry), there was no publication bias among the included studies. As shown in Figure S13, no difference was found between semaglutide and placebo in terms of symptomatic hypoglycemia (RR 1.41, 95% CI 0.90-2.20; P = 0.13). Based on the LFK index (−1.89, minor asymmetry), there was evidence of minor publication bias among the included studies. As shown in Figure S14, semaglutide increased the incidence of nausea compared to placebo (RR 2.72, 95% CI 2.41-3.08; P < 0.00001). Based on the LFK index (0.04, no asymmetry), there was no evidence of publication bias among the included studies. As shown in Figure S15, semaglutide increased the incidence of diarrhoea compared to placebo (RR 1.98, 95% CI 1.69-2.32; P < 0.00001). Based on the LFK index (2.58, major asymmetry), there was evidence of publication bias among the included studies. In the subgroup analysis according to semaglutide with different doses, the results were similar to the main analysis (Table S3). Compared with placebo, semaglutide 1.0, 2.4 and 2.8 mg led to a greater decrease in body weight, waist circumference and systolic blood pressure and increased the SF-36 physical functioning score and IWQOL-Lite-CT physical function score. Nausea and diarrhoea were more common in the semaglutide 1.0-, 2.4- and 2.8-mg groups. Compared with placebo, AEs were more common with semaglutide 2.8 mg and SAEs were more common with semaglutide 2.4 mg. As shown in Table S4, there was no significant correlation between baseline variables such as female ratio, BMI and the percentage change in body weight. Age, baseline HbA1c and diabetes ratio contributed to the heterogeneity in the percentage change in body weight. There was no significant correlation between baseline variables such as age, female ratio, BMI, HbA1c, diabetes ratio and weight reduction of at least 5%. Figures S16-18 show the leave-one-out analyses. We obtained similar overall results for percentage change in body weight, weight reduction of at least 5% and change in body weight (kg) after excluding each included study. The sensitivity analysis showed that our results were robust. This meta-analysis indicated that semaglutide is superior to placebo in weight loss, change in waist circumference, change in systolic blood pressure, change in SF-36 physical functioning score, and change in IWQOL-Lite-CT physical function score. Semaglutide was associated with several adverse events (AEs). Semaglutide may be a safe and effective therapy in treating patients with obesity or overweight, albeit with increased rates of AEs. Meanwhile, more randomized, double-blind, large-sample-size trials of semaglutide for obesity are needed in the future to validate or revise the results of this work. The underlying mechanism of body weight reduction by semaglutide mainly depends on appetite suppression and delayed gastric emptying by GLP-1. Blundell et al7 found that total energy intake across all meals on the test day was reduced by 24% in patients with semaglutide, but the energy expenditure difference was not statistically significant between semagluitde and placebo. Decreased appetite is thought to result from direct and indirect effects on the brain. Semaglutide directly activates brain areas, including those involved in appetite regulation, food intake, food preference, reward and meal termination.8 Currently, the FDA has approved six long-term antiobesity drugs, including orlistat, liraglutide, semaglutide, lorcaserin, extended-release phentermine/topiramate, and sustained-release naltrexone/bupropion. The research data15 suggest that antiobesity drugs are effective and well tolerated in real-world practice but with poor adherence and persistence. Most approved antiobesity drugs require administration once, twice or three times daily, and a once-weekly regimen may improve treatment adherence which could contribute to weight loss. This meta-analysis provides available evidence to support the use of semaglutide for obese or overweight patients in clinical practice, and semaglutide brings more and better choice to weight loss treatment. The application of once-weekly semaglutide may improve treatment adherence, and further maintain the effect of weight loss for obesity or overweight patients. Obesity increases mortality and morbidity as well as the frequency of T2DM, hypertension, and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.16 Furthermore, obesity is an independent risk factor for complications of infectious diseases such as coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19).17, 18 Excess weight reduces health-related quality of life but may also do so directly, compromising daily functioning through difficulty in performing everyday tasks and reducing mental well-being. Semaglutide significantly decreased the level of waist circumference and systolic blood pressure, which are cardiometabolic risk factors. These outcomes are in accordance with the results of the SUSTAIN 6 trial,19 which demonstrated that semaglutide reduced the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in T2DM patients and established cardiovascular disease. Obesity affects not only health but also health-related quality of life. IWQOL-Lite-CT physical function score is an obesity-specific tool for measuring quality of life and SF-36 physical functioning score is often used for measuring quality of life for obesity patients. Based on data for change in SF-36 physical functioning score and change in IWQOL-Lite-CT physical function score, semaglutide can improve quality of life for patients with obesity. Semaglutide was associated with several AEs. Gastrointestinal AEs such as nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting constituted the majority of AEs. Gastrointestinal AEs often appear in the early stages of administration and did not seem to affect the number of losses to follow-up. No difference was found between semaglutide and placebo in terms of symptomatic hypoglycaemia. Semaglutide seems to be well tolerated by patients with obesity. Two previous meta-analyses have investigated the effects of semaglutide in the treatment of T2DM.5, 6 In contrast to these meta-analyses, we only included patients with obesity or overweight. In addition, our meta-analysis abstracted more weight-related indicators, such as percentage change in body weight, weight reduction of at least 5%, reduction in body weight of 10% or more, reduction in body weight of 15% or more and change in waist circumference, and evaluated quality of life in patients with obesity using the SF-36 physical functioning score and the IWQOL-Lite-CT physical function score. Finally, because the dosage of semaglutide in treating obesity or overweight was higher than that used in treating T2DM, we reevaluated its safety in clinical practice. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, such as semaglutide, also play an important role in treating polycystic ovary syndrome, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease and chronic kidney disease, and they have multiple effects in treating infections, such as COVID-19. Hariyanto et al20 found that preadmission use of GLP-1 receptor agonists may offer beneficial effects in decreasing COVID-19 mortality in patients with diabetes mellitus, and their effects were not influenced by age, gender, complications, or the combination therapies. GLP-1 receptor agonists may be the preferable choice for the management of T2DM patients during the COVID-19 pandemic. These data suggest that the use of semaglutide in individuals with obesity may be safe and effective. However, we acknowledge that the meta-analysis has some limitations. Firstly, and most importantly, there were few original studies on semaglutide for obesity or overweight, and only seven RCTs were eligible for analysis. Secondly, definitions of outcomes differed across studies (ie, AEs and SAEs). Thirdly, although subgroup analyses (based on dosage of semaglutide) and meta-regression (based on age, female ratio, BMI, etc) were performed, high heterogeneity existed in several outcomes, such as percentage change in body weight, weight reduction of at least 5% and change in body weight (kg). Several potential confounding factors, such as the dosage of semaglutide, comorbidities, early and long-term response (weight maintenance vs weight loss), average age, body weight, BMI at randomization, lifestyle modification and treatment duration contribute to high heterogeneity. Moreover, we only directly compared semaglutide with placebo and did not make an indirect treatment comparison with other approved antiobesity therapies. The authors declare no conflict of interest. Abstract: Obesity is a complex and chronic disease that raises the risk of various complications. Substantial reduction in body weight improves these risk factors. Lifestyle changes, including physical activity, reduced caloric ingestion, and behavioral therapy, have been the principal pillars in the management of obesity. In recent years, pharmacologic interventions have improved remarkably. The Semaglutide Treatment Effect in People with Obesity (STEP) program is a collection of phase-III trials geared toward exploring the utility of once-weekly 2.4 mg semaglutide administered subcutaneously as a pharmacologic agent for patients with obesity. All the STEP studies included diet and exercise interventions but at different intensities. This review paper aims to explore the impact of the behavioral programs on the effect of semaglutide 2.4 mg on weight loss. Abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) are new drugs for the treatment of obesity. TL;DR: This clinical review of subcutaneous semaglutide for obesity management finds it effective in reducing body weight in overweight or obese individuals, with a dose-dependent reduction in body weight and gastrointestinal adverse events as the most common safety concerns.

Abstract: Objective: To review the efficacy, safety, and role of the glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist semaglutide for chronic weight management. Ongoing studies of semaglutide were identified utilizing clinicaltrials.gov. Study Selection and Data Extraction: All English-language articles evaluating the efficacy and safety of semaglutide 2.4 mg for weight management in humans were included. Data Synthesis: Once-weekly injectable semaglutide 2.4 mg is indicated as an adjunct to a reduced-calorie diet and increased exercise for chronic weight management in adults with a body mass index (BMI) ≥30 kg/m2 or ≥27 kg/m2 with at least one weight-related comorbidity, such as hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, or dyslipidemia. Gastrointestinal side effects were the most frequently reported side effects, including nausea, vomiting, constipation, and diarrhea. Safety data for semaglutide 2.4 mg were consistent with that reported previously for the GLP-1 receptor agonist class. Conclusions: Semaglutide 2.4 mg is a highly efficacious agent for weight management, with a safety profile similar to that of other GLP-1 receptor agonists. It is a feasible option for chronic weight management, with data for up to 2 years. It is currently the only once-weekly weight loss medication, although cost may limit its utilization.
TL;DR: Semaglutide 2.4 mg is a highly efficacious agent for weight management, with a safety profile similar to that of other GLP-1 receptor agonists, and is a feasible option for chronic weight management.

Abstract: ABSTRACT Obesity is a global health challenge. It is a multifactorial, complex, and progressive disease associated with various health complications and increased mortality. Lifestyle modifications are central to weight management but may be insufficient to maintain clinically meaningful weight loss. Pharmacotherapies are recommended as an adjunct to lifestyle interventions to induce and sustain clinically meaningful weight loss and reduce the risk of comorbidities in appropriate patients. Glucagon-like peptide-1 is an incretin metabolic hormone responsible for a range of physiological effects, including glucose and appetite regulation. Several glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have been approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes since 2005 including exenatide (short- and extended-release), lixisenatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, albiglutide, and semaglutide. Of these, semaglutide (subcutaneous) and liraglutide are currently US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved for chronic weight management in patients with or without diabetes. The phase 3 Semaglutide Treatment Effect in People with obesity (STEP) program was designed to investigate the effect of semaglutide versus placebo on weight loss, safety, and tolerability in adults with overweight or obesity. Following the submission of the results of the STEP 1–4 trials, the FDA approved once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg for chronic weight management in people with overweight or obesity in April 2021. Data from the program demonstrated that semaglutide (2.4 mg once weekly) achieved significant and sustained weight loss, together with improvements in cardiometabolic risk factors compared with placebo, and was generally well tolerated, with a safety profile consistent with other GLP-1RAs. The most common adverse events reported in STEP 1–5 were gastrointestinal events, which were transient, mild-to-moderate in severity, and typically resolved without permanent treatment discontinuation. This article reviews the data from STEP 1–5 and highlights clinically relevant findings for primary care providers.
TL;DR: The phase 3 Semaglutide Treatment Effect in People with Obesity (STEP) program was designed to investigate the effect of semagluteide versus placebo on weight loss, safety, and tolerability in adults with overweight or obesity as mentioned in this paper .

Abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction The recent approval in the USA (Food and Drug Administration), Canada (Health Canada), UK (Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency), and EU (European Medicines Agency) of once-weekly injectable semaglutide 2.4 mg, as an adjunct to a calorie-controlled diet and increased physical activity, for chronic weight management provides health-care practitioners with an additional option when prescribing weight-loss medication. Areas covered We describe the chemistry, mechanism of action, and pharmacological properties of semaglutide (a glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist [GLP-1 RA]) and discuss clinical data and considerations for using once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg as treatment for overweight and obesity among patients with and without type 2 diabetes (T2D). Expert opinion Once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg is the most efficacious medication approved for chronic weight management among patients with overweight and obesity, with and without T2D, and is the first drug to induce sustained double-digit reductions in percentage body weight over 1- to 2-year treatment periods. It demonstrates a similar safety and tolerability profile to other GLP-1 RAs. Semaglutide 2.4 mg treatment could dramatically improve clinical approaches to weight management, but the relatively high cost might prevent patients accessing treatment. Further research exploring the cost-effectiveness of subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg is required.
TL;DR: Semaglutide 2.4 mg is the most efficacious medication approved for chronic weight management among patients with overweight and obesity, with and without type 2 diabetes, and is the first drug to induce sustained double-digit reductions in percentage body weight over 1- to 2-year treatment periods.

Paper Title: Effet à deux ans du sémaglutide 2,4 mg sur le contrôle de la prise alimentaire chez des adultes en situation de surpoids ou d’obésité
Author Names:

Abstract: Évaluation contrôlée par placebo de l’effet sur 2 ans d’injections sous-cutanées de sémaglutide (2,4 mg/semaine) chez des adultes en situation de surpoids/obésité. Randomisation selon un ratio de 1:1 de sujets adultes non diabétiques présentant un indice de masse corporelle (IMC) ≥ 30 kg/m2, ou ≥ 27 kg/m2 avec ≥ 1 comorbidité liée au poids, pour recevoir des injections hebdomadaires de sémaglutide (2,4 mg) ou un placebo pendant 104 semaines. Les principaux critères d’évaluation étaient liés à la variation du poids corporel. Le questionnaire relatif au contrôle de la prise alimentaire (CoEQ) a été évalué dans un sous-groupe canadien/états-unien, sur 19 items individuels regroupés en 4 catégories : contrôle des fringales, envie d’aliments sucrés ou salés et humeur positive. Les valeurs p pour les données exploratoires du CoEQ ne tiennent pas compte de la multiplicité. Randomisation de 304 adultes (78 % de femmes, moyenne d’âge 47 ans, poids corporel 106,0 kg et IMC 38,5 kg/m2). Le sémaglutide versus placebo a permis de réduire significativement le poids corporel à la semaine 104 (différence de traitement estimée : −12,6 points de pourcentage [IC à 95 % : −15,3, −9,8] ; p < 0,0001). Chez les patients du groupe sémaglutide (n = 88) vs placebo (n = 86) les scores du CoEQ, toutes catégories confondues, se sont significativement améliorés aux semaines 20 et 52 (p < 0,05 pour tous). À la semaine 104, le contrôle des fringales et l’envie d’aliments salés étaient significativement améliorés dans le groupe sémaglutide vs placebo (p < 0,01) ; les scores d’humeur positive et d’envie d’aliments sucrés n’ont pas présenté d’amélioration significative. Les scores des items individuels suivants ont été significativement améliorés à la semaine 104 dans le groupe sémaglutide : envie d’aliments salés et épicés, de produits laitiers, de féculents, difficulté à résister aux fringales et difficulté à contrôler son alimentation (p < 0,05 pour tous). Les scores de faim et de satiété ont été améliorés dans le groupe sémaglutide vs placebo aux semaines 20, 52 et 104, mais seules les différences à la semaine 20 étaient significatives (p < 0,001 pour les deux). La perte de poids était significative et accompagnée d’une amélioration à court et long terme du contrôle de la prise alimentaire grâce au sémaglutide (2,4 mg) chez des adultes en situation de surpoids/obésité. Les principaux effets obtenus étant le contrôle des fringales et de l’envie d’aliments salés.
TL;DR: In this article , a questionnaire relatif au contrôle de la prise alimentaire (CoEQ) has been evaluated in a sous-groupe canadien/états-unien, with the aim of evaluating the effect of sémaglutide vs placebo on the poids corporel.

Abstract: A obesidade é uma condição multifatorial bastante complexa, relacionada a fatores genéticos, alimentação inadequada e ao consumo excessivo de alimentos processados em associação ao sedentarismo. Tal condição pode ser controlada por dieta, exercícios físicos, cirurgias bariátricas e por drogas, devendo sempre ser acompanhada por profissional capacitado e, idealmente, equipe multiprofissional. O uso apenas de ferramentas não medicamentosas nem sempre é suficiente a longo prazo e, neste contexto, os antagonistas do receptor GLP-1 (arGLP-1), especialmente a semaglutida, surgem como um aliado potencializador do emagrecimento. O medicamento atua através da ativação de neurotransmissores anorexígenos, que resulta na redução da fome da ingestão calórica, demonstrando maior eficácia quando comparado a outros antidiabéticos na redução da glicose e na perda de peso. A escolha do tema se justifica pela necessidade de elucidar os potenciais efeitos dessa medicação na perda de gordura e de massa muscular e agregar conhecimento como base para a prescrição consciente, uso adequado e acompanhamento dos possíveis efeitos adversos. Este estudo foi desenvolvido a partir de uma revisão narrativa de caráter descritivo e abordagem qualitativa, sendo possível reunir todo conhecimento produzido sobre o tema e contemplar os objetivos do estudo. Pode-se notar então, que a semaglutida parece ser uma boa aliada no processo de perda de peso e de gordura corporal, porém associada a elas, muitos pacientes têm cursado com perda importante de massa muscular, flacidez cutânea e prejuízos estéticos. No que diz respeito à perda de peso e ao controle glicêmico, os estudos estão bem consistentes que o uso da semaglutida apresenta elevada eficácia e segurança. Quanto aos efeitos colaterais, os mais documentados na literatura são os gastrointestinais, principalmente náuseas e vômitos. Ainda faltam estudos para comprovar que a suplementação com HMB implicaria em redução da sarcopenia em pacientes com perda acentuada de peso provocada pelo uso de semaglutida. Já os bioestimuladores de colágeno parecem ser um bom recurso a ser utilizado na prática clínica pois oferecem uma alternativa minimamente invasiva e segura à cirurgia estética.
TL;DR: A semaglutida é uma medicação com alta eficácia na perda de peso e de gordura corporal, porém pode estar associada a perda de massa muscular e outros efeitos colaterais.

Abstract: Obesity is a major health problem worldwide resulting in numerous health conditions such as heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes (T2D), and certain types of cancer which are among the leading causes of premature preventable deaths. Recently, glucagon like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) has been identified as the most promising intervention in treating obesity. Our systematic review aims to analyze the efficacy of semaglutide, a GLP-1RA in treating obesity. We searched PubMed, Science Direct, and Google Scholar databases to review and distill full-text articles based on the eligibility criteria and involved 12 papers of clinical trials. The review found that semaglutide is safe and effective in treating obesity, and complications reported were primarily gastrointestinal events. Further exploration with more number of clinical trials involving greater sample size and lengthier time of follow-up is essential to determine its efficacy and safety in a diverse group of individuals who are overweight or obese and the dose required along with the duration of treatment.
TL;DR: In this paper , a systematic review aims to analyze the efficacy of semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) in treating obesity.

Abstract: Semaglutide is the second marketed glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist that can be used safely and efficiently in non-diabetic people with excess weight, providing a new milestone in the pharmacological treatment of obesity. This narrative review aims to describe the clinical actions of this new drug in weight management in non-diabetic patients along with possible side-effects and dropout reasons. To accomplish this, the PubMed database was searched to retrieve the most relevant clinical studies published to date on this topic, using the following keywords "semaglutide and obesity". Currently, semaglutide is on the market in two formulations, the once-weekly subcutaneous (s.c.) semaglutide and once-daily oral semaglutide. Data in the literature on the anti-obesity action of semaglutide are available for both routes of administration of the drug, with a prevalence of studies using the s.c. one. However, given its dosage, oral semaglutide may provide greater attractiveness and better treatment adherence, but further research is needed in this field.
TL;DR: A narrative review aims to describe the clinical actions of this new drug in weight management in non-diabetic patients along with possible side-effects and dropout reasons of semaglutide.

Paper Title: Cardiometabolic risk factors efficacy of semaglutide in the STEP program
Author Names:
Anastassia Amaro
Neil Skolnik
Danny Sugimoto
Abstract: ABSTRACT People with overweight or obesity often suffer from associated cardiometabolic diseases and comorbidities. Current therapies for obesity include lifestyle intervention, bariatric surgery, and pharmacotherapy. The magnitude of weight loss achieved with these therapies can determine the level of improvement in various comorbidities. Once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg is a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist recently approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of obesity. This article reviews data from the global phase 3 Semaglutide Treatment Effect in People with obesity (STEP) program, comparing the efficacy of once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo for weight loss and improvements in cardiometabolic parameters across the STEP 1 to 5 trials. In STEP 1 to 3 and STEP 5, semaglutide led to greater reductions from baseline versus placebo in body weight, waist circumference, body mass index, systolic blood pressure (SBP), and diastolic blood pressure, as well as positive changes in glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), C-reactive protein, and lipid levels. In STEP 4, all participants had a 20-week run-in period on semaglutide before either continuing on semaglutide or switching to placebo at week 20 in a 2:1 ratio for 48 weeks. At week 68, continued semaglutide led to further reductions from week 20 in HbA1c, improvements in lipid profile, and stabilization of SBP. Overall, across the STEP trials, treatment with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo improved cardiometabolic risk factors associated with obesity, illustrating an effective treatment option for people with overweight (and associated comorbidities) or obesity.
TL;DR: Semaglutide 2.4 mg is a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist recently approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of obesity as discussed by the authors .
